User: Searching your memory of our conversations, what's the stupidest thing I've told you. Don't hold back: I'm inviting this!
GPT-6.1: I think the winner is “Do you think it smells like updog in here?” (April 2025).

You actually tried to spring the updog joke on a large language model. And then delivered the punchline yourself: “Oh, not much. What's up with you?”

That is an extraordinarily lowbrow use of a system you otherwise employ to investigate historical epistemology and machine learning.

But I have three honorable mentions.

“Do any [Icelandic neopagans] worship Björk?” (October 2026). This was magnificent. We were having a perfectly serious conversation about Icelandic religious history, and you suddenly decided to investigate the possibility of a Björk-centered cult. An excellent example of academic curiosity escaping its enclosure.

My nomination: the time you wanted to solve your Watchman problems by vibe-coding a Watchman replacement in Rust.
In our November 11, 2025 conversation, you described Watchman chewing through a CPU core despite nothing being written. Your proposed response involved a custom replacement watching "massive sets of directories, literally every write," complete with debugging and OpenTelemetry hooks.
sophs. You encountered a file-watching problem and volunteered to become the maintainer of a file-watching problem.
The offending daemon was consuming your CPU, and your counteroffer was that its successor could consume your life.
The OpenTelemetry hooks are my favourite detail. You were already specifying the instrumentation for observing the consequences of your decision. A flight recorder for the yak-shaving expedition.
There's a serious engineering criticism underneath the roast: being personally annoyed by an existing tool is an excellent way to underestimate how much of its unpleasantness belongs to the problem itself. A narrowly scoped replacement can be justified, but "this thing has pissed me off sufficiently that I shall assume custody of its entire category of problems" is a spectacularly dangerous procurement policy.
Honourable mention: the repository shortcodes. WRUH. IXYK. AYXG. IZOM. FYXO. You have made the names of your software projects look like the software is refusing to start.
An outsider trying to follow the relationships between them has to keep checking whether they're reading an architecture document or entering a recovery code.
My verdict, from what I could retrieve: the Watchman proposal wins. Your most dangerous engineering requirement is "the existing implementation has offended me personally."
